newsitem.title: UK: U.S. tobacco deal not enough, journal complains.
newsitem.headline: U.S. tobacco deal not enough, journal complains.

text.p: A tentative settlement reached with tobacco companies in the United States does not go far enough, the internationally respected medical journal the Lancet complained on Friday.

It said the $368 billion deal, which severely restricts cigarette advertising and under which the industry agreed to recognise the authority of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), seemed impressive at first.
"But on closer inspection the proposal is full of loopholes," the Lancet said in an editorial.
"The pact as written is clearly not acceptable," it added.
"It is unlikely that the agreement, if it is approved by Congress and the president, will significantly reduce tobacco-related death and disease in the USA."

For example, it said, the agreement required tobacco companies to give millions to campaigns aimed at discouraging teenagers from smoking. If teenage smoking rates did not fall, the industry would have to pay penalties.
But the penalties could be recouped by adding just a few cents to the price of a packet of cigarettes -- hardly a disincentive.

"Most worryingly, the agreement undermines the FDA's ability to regulate tobacco," the Lancet added. "The proposal accepts the FDA's authority to regulate nicotine but would prevent the agency banning nicotine from tobacco for 12 years."
It would also make "impossible" requirements such as making the FDA show substantial evidence that nicotine is harmful to health before it would require levels to be reduced.
"People smoke not because of the Marlboro Man but because they crave nicotine," the editorial went on.

"The only way to reduce the damage done by smoking is for the FDA to retain the authority and have the funding to develop a scientific programme that will statutorily reduce and eventually eliminate nicotine from tobacco."
President Bill Clinton and members of Congress have also said they were worried that the FDA could be paralysed by the agreement, which could take months to get Congressional approval.
The Lancet added: "The agreement also does nothing to stop U.S. tobacco companies selling hard in countries that lack the means to defend themselves."
Anti-tobacco lobbyists have complained that the agreement only covers the United States, which accounts for only a small percentage of tobacco company profits.
On Thursday, Mississippi became the first of 40 U.S. states to settle its suit against the industry.
